**Bracket signatures hide mismatched closers inside newly opened pairs**

`checkFix` can accept a syntactically invalid replacement when a mismatched closer has the same signature as a leading orphan closer. Distinguish mismatched closers on a nonempty stack from leading orphan closers, and always reject the former.

Distinguish closers encountered with a nonempty, mismatched stack from leading orphan closers and reject the former regardless of the reference signature.

Confirmed on this branch: with `existingCode` `}.property('a')`, `checkFix` passes the fix `x(}).property('b')` (null), while `main` flags it. A closer that mismatches a non-empty stack is broken whatever the reference; only a closer met with an empty stack is an orphan the original can share.

Agreed, and the asymmetry you're drawing is the right one. The criterion isn't a token-count comparison against `existingCode` or a per-type lookup — it's purely the stack state at the moment the closer is consumed, replaying the combined stream:

- **stack empty → orphan.** This is the only class the original can excuse, by analogy with an orphan of its own.
- **stack non-empty, top matches → legitimate close**, including one that closes an opener living in `existingCode` (the cross-boundary case fixes need).
- **stack non-empty, top mismatches → hard failure.** Nothing in the reference can excuse it, because the fix itself opened something this closer doesn't close.

So with `existingCode` `}.property('a')` and fix `x(}).property('b')`, the `}` should be rejected everywhere: `(` is on the stack when it arrives, so it's a mismatch, not a shareable orphan. `main` flagging it is correct; the branch returning `null` is the regression. My guess is the branch collapsed the check into a per-type count or type-only match against the reference, which will happily pair a fix's *mismatched* closer with the original's orphan — exactly the case your rule forbids.

Worth locking this in with a regression test that pairs it with a positive control: same `existingCode`, but a fix whose closer genuinely hits an empty stack, which must still be accepted. That way the test fails whichever direction the check drifts.

Two edges to pin down while you're in there: must a shared orphan match token type, and is a fix closer that closes an opener from `existingCode` still classified as a legitimate close rather than a mismatch?

**Fix truncated inside an unterminated block comment is now published**

An unterminated `/*` block comment now survives the signature-equality rescue, so everything after it is commented out when the fix is applied. Reject the fix when `/*` remains in `nonLiteral` after complete `/*...*/` pairs are stripped, as the suite already does for unterminated literals.

````text
The new signature-equality rescue accepts any fix whose bracket imbalance matches the quoted lines, including a generation cut off inside an UNTERMINATED `/*` block comment — e.g. `checkFix('if (a) {\n run();', 'if (a) {\n run();\n /* retry the call')` returns `null` because `stripComments` only removes closed `/*...*/` pairs, so the surviving `/*` leaves the fix's `|{` signature equal to the reference's. The published fix is applied verbatim, so everything after `/* retry the call` is commented out to the end of the file (the tail check cannot see it — the text ends in a letter — and the unterminated-quote scan never inspects comments); before this change that same input was rejected as `truncated` because the open `{` was the only signal, and the suite already treats an unterminated literal as truncation regardless of what the reference looks like. Add the same unconditional signal for block comments — reject the fix when a `/*` survives in `nonLiteral` after complete `/*...*/` pairs have been stripped (string-literal content is already removed there, so `const s = "/*"` is not affected).
````

One note for the record, since the suggestion wasn't a regression claim: its point was that the recovery stays partial for a common cut shape. A quote that cuts an argument list, object literal, or array ends on `,`, and a fix that reproduces that line verbatim still trips the operator-tail check — so it still comes back `truncated` and takes the downgrade path in `agent-review.stage.ts` (cleared `improvedCode`, plain comment, bad-fix notice). If you want that gap tracked rather than lost, I can open a Kody issue on kodus-ai to make the tail checks reference-aware (the same-signature exemption brackets now get) as a follow-up.

These are guards on behaviour that must not change ("flags …" / "still flags …"), so passing before the change is expected. The block-comment case at `:106-110` does fail on 5f45c5ab3d, the commit before this one.

"Cut the same way" refers to the inherited open `{`: the case shows an inherited bracket imbalance does not excuse an unclosed string. Comparing the string check against the reference is not something this PR does or needs.

@pcbeingused333 this one is real. A fix that adds a `dir/*` glob in a language without `/* */` comments is now flagged, while main accepts it:

- Dockerfile: `COPY build/ /app/` → `COPY dist/* /app/`: main `null`, this branch `truncated`
- Makefile: `rm -f build/x.o` → `rm -f build/*.o`: main `null`, this branch `truncated`
- bash: `cp build/a out/` → `cp dist/* out/`: main `null`, this branch `truncated`

Only run the dangling-`/*` check for languages that have block comments (C family, JS/TS, Java, Go, Rust, CSS, PHP, Kotlin, Swift, C#, SQL), and add these three as accepted cases in `is-usable-fix.spec.ts`.

Got it — that clears up the ambiguity. "Cut the same way" is about the inherited open `{` being the same underlying condition, not about the two checks behaving identically. And the case is the useful part: an inherited bracket imbalance doesn't excuse an unclosed string — the string still has to terminate, and the diagnostic should fire regardless of what the bracket context looks like.

On comparing the string check against the reference: agreed, that's outside the scope of this PR. Nothing in the change depends on that comparison, and pulling it in would turn a focused fix into a broader validation exercise. If we ever want that coverage, a separate issue is the cleaner route.

If reviewers keep tripping on the distinction, a single test with an inherited `{` plus an unclosed string — asserting the string diagnostic still appears — would pin the semantics down. But if the current coverage already captures it, there's no reason to expand the diff.

<!-- kody-codereview -->

Right — that's the expected shape. The `flags …` / `still flags …` guards are there to lock in behavior that's supposed to stay put, so them being green on both sides is the signal you want, not evidence they're inert. The block-comment case at `:106-110` is the only one actually coupled to the change, and it failing on 5f45c5ab3d is what makes it a real test rather than a decision that happens to pass.

The one thing I'd want to eyeball before signing off is *why* it fails on the parent commit — ideally an assertion about block-comment handling, not something incidental like a fixture that didn't exist yet, an import error, or a syntax error in the test file itself. That kind of failure would still show a red-to-green transition without ever exercising the new code path. If the failure output points at the behavior under test, then the before/after pair holds up.

````text
Language allowlist regex misses the u flag and canonicalization

The new `blockCommentLanguage` test matches `language` with a case-insensitive regex that has no `u` flag and hands it the raw `language.trim()` without canonicalizing invisible characters first. The rule requires names to be canonicalized (strip `\p{Cf}` format characters) before matching and case-insensitive validation regexes to carry the `u` flag so Unicode case folding applies (U+017F folds to `s` only with `u`). As written, a language value carrying a zero-width space or a Unicode case-look-alike character fails the test, `blockCommentLanguage` becomes false, and the dangling-`/*` truncation guard is skipped for a language that does have block comments — a fix cut inside a block comment then ships as usable and, when applied, comments out the rest of the file. Strip format characters from the trimmed value and add the `u` flag: `/^(?:...|sql)$/iu.test(language.trim().replace(/\p{Cf}/gu, ''))`.
````
